blocks.html: In Arguments and Non-Arguments you learned to tell an argument from a plain claim. Traditional logic starts one step further back. It asks what the mind is doing when it thinks at all, and it finds three different acts, each building on the one before.

items: Simple apprehension: grasping what something is, such as "triangle" or "the oak by the river". Its product is a term.
Judgment: joining two terms and affirming or denying one of the other, such as "The oak is tall." Its product is a proposition.
Reasoning: moving from propositions we hold to a new one, such as "All oaks are trees, and this is an oak, so this is a tree." Its product is an argument.

blocks.html: A term only names. A proposition affirms or denies, so it can be true or false. An argument draws a conclusion from premises, so it can be valid or invalid.

Each act needs the one before it. You cannot judge that the oak is tall until you have grasped "oak" and "tall". You cannot reason to a conclusion until you have judgments to reason from. That is why this course follows the same order: terms first (this unit), then propositions (units 2 to 4), then reasoning (units 5 to 7).

blocks.html: In The Three Acts of the Mind you met the term as the product of simple apprehension. A term is a word or phrase that names a class of things or one individual thing. In a proposition, terms are the building blocks that the verb joins.

A singular term names exactly one thing ("Mount Everest", "the tallest student in our class"). A general term names a class, so it applies to each of its members ("mountains", "students who play the violin"). Count ideas, not words.

Logic cares about what a phrase picks out, not how long it is. "The first president of the United States" uses seven words, but it names one person, so it works exactly like a name. "Dogs" is one word, but it applies to millions of animals. When we later ask whether a statement is about all of a class or only some of it, we need to know which phrases name classes.

blocks.html: A term does two jobs at once. It points to things, and it carries an idea of what those things are like. Traditional logic gives each job a name.

The extension of a term is the set of things it applies to. Its comprehension (also called intension) is the set of features it implies. Add a feature, and the comprehension grows while the extension shrinks or stays the same.

Every feature you add is one more test a thing must pass. "Dog" applies to every dog. "Black dog" applies only to the dogs that also pass the "black" test, so fewer things fit. "Small black dog" adds a third test, and fewer still pass. The tests pile up (comprehension grows) as the crowd that passes them thins out (extension shrinks). If every member already had the feature, the crowd stays the same size, which is why we say "shrinks or stays the same".

blocks.html: You saw in Extension and Comprehension that terms nest inside one another, and in Definition by Genus and Difference that a definition names a wider class and then narrows it. Logic names the two ends of that relation.
A genus is a wider class that is divided into narrower classes; each narrower class is a species of that genus. The same class can be a species of one genus and a genus of other species.

Genus and species name a relation between two classes, like "parent" and "child". Nobody is a parent all by themselves; you are a parent of someone. In the same way, "polygon" is a species when we compare it with "shape" (every polygon is a shape, not every shape is a polygon), and a genus when we compare it with "triangle". Only the comparison decides.

blocks.title: One class, two roles
blocks.q: How is "mammals" related to "animals" and to "dogs"?
steps: Compare mammals with animals: every mammal is an animal, but some animals (birds, fish) are not mammals. So mammals is the narrower class: a species of animals.
Compare mammals with dogs: every dog is a mammal, but not every mammal is a dog. So mammals is the wider class: a genus of dogs.

blocks.html: Porphyry drew these nested classes as a tree, now called the Tree of Porphyry: substance at the top, then body, living body, animal, and rational animal (human being) near the bottom. A class with no wider class above it is a highest genus; a class that is not divided any further is a lowest species. Everything between is both a genus and a species.

Using the biology ranks. In biology, "genus" and "species" are fixed levels (Canis is a genus, Canis familiaris a species). In logic they are relative: any wider class is a genus of any narrower class inside it, at any level. Check by asking "wider or narrower than what?"

blocks.html: Once you know genus and species, you can sort every true statement "Every S is P" by how the predicate belongs to the subject. Since Porphyry wrote about them in the third century, logicians have counted five ways, called the predicables.

blocks.cap: The five predicables, with one subject.

blocks.html: Genus, difference and species belong to what a thing is. A property is not part of the definition but always comes with it. An accident could be missing without the thing changing its kind.

The test for each is a question. Is it the wider class? (genus) Is it what marks this kind off from others in that class? (difference) Is it both together? (species) If it is none of those, could a member of the kind lack it? If no member could lack it, because it follows from what the thing is, it is a property. If a member could lack it and still be the same kind of thing, it is an accident.

blocks.title: A property
blocks.q: Subject: square. Predicate: "has diagonals that cross at right angles". Which predicable?
steps: It is not the genus (rectangle), not the difference (four equal sides), and not the full definition.
Could a square lack it? No: every square has such diagonals, because of what a square is.
So it is a property.

blocks.title: An accident
blocks.q: Subject: rectangle. Predicate: "is 4 cm long". Which predicable?
steps: It is not part of the definition, and it does not follow from it.
A rectangle 5 cm long is just as much a rectangle. So it can be missing: an accident.

blocks.html: Confusing property and accident. Both lie outside the definition, so they look alike. The test: a property belongs to every member because of what the thing is (every triangle's angles add up to 180°); an accident does not (this triangle happens to be red). Ask "could one of them lack it?"

blocks.html: Definition moves up from a species to its genus. Logical division moves down: it splits a genus into its species. Done well, it gives a clean map of a subject; done badly, it causes the confusion you see in messy categories.
A good division uses one principle, so its parts are exclusive (nothing falls in two parts) and together exhaustive (everything falls in some part).

A principle is one question that sorts every member: "What is the largest angle of this triangle?" Because each triangle has exactly one answer, it lands in exactly one part, so no overlaps; and because every triangle has some answer, none are left out. Mixing two questions, such as kind of writing and type of binding for books, breaks both: a hardcover novel lands in two parts, and some books may land in none.

blocks.html: A statement is true or false. A categorical proposition is a statement of one special shape: it relates two classes, named by terms, by saying that one is included in the other or shut out of it, in whole or in part.
Every categorical proposition in standard form has four parts, in this order:

items: the quantifier: All, No or Some;
the subject term: the class the statement is about;
the copula: are or are not;
the predicate term: the class the subject is related to.

blocks.name: lg-syllogism

premises: All whales are mammals that breathe air

blocks.cap: The four parts of a standard-form categorical proposition.

blocks.html: Standard form is Quantifier – subject term – copula – predicate term, with both terms naming classes: "All whales are mammals that breathe air."

Fixing one shape lets us compare statements part by part. Once every claim reads "All/No/Some ___ are (not) ___", we can see at a glance which two classes it relates and how, and the rest of this course (the square, conversion, syllogisms) works on those parts. The terms must name classes ("mammals that breathe air", not "breathe air") so that both sides of the copula are the same kind of thing.

blocks.title: Finding the terms
blocks.q: Name the four parts of "Some books on the top shelf are not novels by Jane Austen."
steps: Quantifier: the first word, Some.
Subject term: everything between the quantifier and the copula: books on the top shelf.
Copula: are not.
Predicate term: everything after the copula: novels by Jane Austen.
blocks.a: Some / books on the top shelf / are not / novels by Jane Austen

blocks.html: Taking the grammatical subject or the verb for the logical terms. In "All whales are mammals that breathe air", the predicate term is the whole phrase mammals that breathe air, not "mammals" and not "breathe". Check: the predicate term is everything after "are" or "are not".
In an E proposition ("No dogs are cats") the word "no" belongs to the quantifier, so the copula is plain are. Only the O form ("Some dogs are not puppies") has are not.

blocks.html: Quantity asks "all or some?": A and E are universal, I and O particular. Quality asks "including or excluding?": A and I are affirmative, E and O negative. In logic, some means "at least one".

"Some" means at least one because logic only keeps what a statement guarantees. "Some students passed" guarantees that at least one did. It does not guarantee that some failed; the speaker may simply not know. If all of them passed, "Some students passed" is still true, just not the whole story.

blocks.html: Everyday speech rarely uses the exact words of the four forms. Before you can test reasoning, you rewrite each statement in standard form. The meaning must stay the same; only the wording changes.

blocks.html: Three steps: (1) make the verb "are" plus a class ("bark" → "are barkers"); (2) choose the quantifier from the meaning: all, none, at least one, or at least one not; (3) write it as All/No/Some S are (not) P. "Many" and "most" become "some". A statement about one named thing becomes a universal about a one-member class.

Standard form has only four quantifiers, so every everyday quantifier must map to the one that keeps what it guarantees. "Most" guarantees at least one, so it becomes "some" (we lose information, but we never add any). A singular statement such as "Maya is a hiker" says something about every member of a class with exactly one member, so it acts as a universal: "All people identical to Maya are hikers."

blocks.html: Some words in everyday statements change the order of the terms. The most important is only.

"Only S are P" and "None but S are P" become All P are S (swap the terms). "The only S are P" becomes All S are P (keep the order). "All except S are P" makes two claims: All non-S are P, and No S are P.

"Only members may vote" sets a requirement on voters: to vote, you must be a member. That is a claim about every voter: all voters are members. It says nothing about every member; some members may stay home. So the class after "only" is the one the other class must fit inside, and it becomes the predicate. "The only" works the other way: "The only animals in the canyon are skunks" says every animal in the canyon is a skunk.

blocks.html: Look again at the four forms. Some of them say something about every member of a class; others speak about only part of it. A term is distributed in a proposition when the proposition says something about every member of the class it names.

blocks.cap: Universals distribute the subject; negatives distribute the predicate.

blocks.html: Universal statements (A, E) distribute their subject. Negative statements (E, O) distribute their predicate. So A distributes S, E both, I neither, O only P.

Take each form in turn. "All S are P" speaks of every S, but only of the P that happen to be S. "No S are P" shuts every S out of the whole of P, which says of every P that it is not an S: both terms. "Some S are P" speaks of at least one S and at least one P: neither class as a whole. "Some S are not P" speaks of only some S, but says that whole class P leaves those S out, so it tells us something about every P: the predicate.

blocks.html: A Venn diagram for "All S are P" shades region 1 and puts no X anywhere. So the picture does not say that any S exist. That raises a real question: does "All S are P" claim that there are S?

On the modern (Boolean) reading, A and E say nothing about whether the subject class has members; only I and O assert that something exists. On the traditional (Aristotelian) reading, every statement assumes its subject class is not empty.

Consider "All trespassers will be prosecuted." The sign is true even if no one ever trespasses: it says there are no unprosecuted trespassers, not that trespassers exist. That is the Boolean reading of A: an empty region, nothing more. "Some trespassers were prosecuted", by contrast, says at least one exists. The traditional reading instead adds an assumption to every statement, which suits talk about familiar classes (birds, books) and fails for empty ones (unicorns).

blocks.html: Take one pair of terms, say birds and swimmers, and write all four forms with them. Those four statements are not independent: the truth of one limits the truth of the others. Since late antiquity, logicians have drawn those limits as a square.

blocks.name: lg-square
blocks.cap: The square of opposition for birds and swimmers.

items: Corners: universals on top (A left, E right), particulars below (I under A, O under E). Affirmatives on the left, negatives on the right.
Contradictories (the diagonals, A–O and E–I): exactly one is true.
Contraries (the top, A–E): not both true.
Subcontraries (the bottom, I–O): not both false.
Subalterns (the sides, A–I and E–O): truth flows down, falsity flows up.

blocks.html: The square names four relations among A, E, I and O with the same terms: contradictories, contraries, subcontraries and subalterns. This traditional square assumes the subject class has members.

The layout follows quantity and quality. Moving across a side changes quality (affirmative to negative); moving up or down changes quantity (universal to particular); a diagonal changes both. A statement and its full opposite, different in both ways, can never agree, which is why the diagonals are the strongest relation. Later lessons show why each side behaves as it does.

blocks.title: Naming a relation
blocks.q: How are "No birds are swimmers" and "Some birds are swimmers" related?
steps: The first is E (top right). The second is I (bottom left).
Top right to bottom left is a diagonal.

blocks.html: The names come from the old Latin textbooks: contraries are opposed at the top, subcontraries sit "under" them at the bottom, and a subaltern is the statement "below another" on the same side.

Placing the corners in the wrong spots, so every relation comes out wrong. Remember: universals on top, A left and E right; I sits under A and O under E (each particular under the universal with the same quality). Check: the two left corners both affirm; the two right corners both deny.

blocks.html: On the square of opposition, the diagonals join A with O and E with I. These pairs are contradictories.

Contradictories cannot both be true and cannot both be false: exactly one of them is true. The contradictory of "All S are P" is "Some S are not P"; the contradictory of "No S are P" is "Some S are P".

Each pair talks about the same region of a Venn diagram and says opposite things about it. "All S are P" says region 1 (S outside P) is empty; "Some S are not P" says region 1 has something in it. A region is either empty or not, so exactly one of the two is right. The same goes for E and I with region 2. Because this reason uses no assumption about existence, the contradictories hold on every reading.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: A shades region 1; O puts an X in region 1. Exactly one can be right.

blocks.title: Denying a universal
blocks.q: What is the contradictory of "All the cookies are burned"? (Standard form: All cookies on the tray are burned cookies.)
steps: It is an A statement, so its contradictory is the O with the same terms.
To show that not all the cookies are burned, you only need one cookie that is not.
blocks.a: Some cookies on the tray are not burned cookies.

blocks.title: Denying a negative
blocks.q: What is the contradictory of "No hikers are poets"?
steps: It is an E statement, so its contradictory is the I with the same terms.
To show that "none" is wrong, one hiker who is a poet is enough.

blocks.html: Giving "No S are P" as the contradictory of "All S are P". That is the contrary, and both can be false at once (some cookies burned, some not). To deny "all", you need only "some are not". Check: could your two statements both be false? If yes, they are not contradictories.

blocks.html: The diagonals are the strongest link on the square. The top and bottom sides are weaker, and each is weak in its own way.
Contraries (A and E) cannot both be true, but can both be false. Subcontraries (I and O) cannot both be false, but can both be true. (Traditional reading: the subject class has members.)

Picture a class where some members are P and some are not: some students swim and some do not. Then "All students are swimmers" and "No students are swimmers" are both false, and "Some are" and "Some are not" are both true. That mixed case is why contraries can both be false and subcontraries both true. But if there is at least one student, the A and the E cannot both be true (that student cannot be both a swimmer and not one), and the I and the O cannot both be false (that student is one or the other).

head: Pair
Both true?
Both false?

blocks.name: lg-square
blocks.cap: If A is false, E is undetermined: contraries can both be false.

blocks.title: From a true contrary
blocks.q: "All the students are swimmers" is true. What about "No students are swimmers"?
steps: A and E are contraries: they cannot both be true.
A is true, so E must be false.

blocks.title: From a false subcontrary
blocks.q: "Some students are swimmers" is false. What about "Some students are not swimmers"?
steps: I and O are subcontraries: they cannot both be false.
I is false, so O must be true.

blocks.html: Treating contraries as contradictories and concluding from "A is false" that E is true. Both can be false when some S are P and some are not. Check by building the mixed case: if it makes both statements false, you cannot conclude anything from one being false.

blocks.html: The last relation on the square runs down the sides: from A to I and from E to O. Each universal is the superaltern, and the particular below it with the same quality is its subaltern.

On the traditional square, truth flows down (if A is true, I is true; if E is true, O is true) and falsity flows up (if I is false, A is false; if O is false, E is false). Everything else is undetermined.

If every one of the students is a swimmer, and there is at least one student (the traditional assumption), then at least one student is a swimmer: truth flows down. If not even one student is a swimmer, then certainly not all of them are: falsity flows up. But "some are" does not make "all are" true, and "not all are" does not make "some are" false, so truth does not flow up and falsity does not flow down.

blocks.name: lg-square
blocks.cap: E true sends truth down to O, and makes A false (contraries) and I false (contradictories).

blocks.title: Truth down
blocks.q: "No birdwatchers are early risers" is true. What follows about "Some birdwatchers are not early risers"?
steps: E and O are subalterns, with E on top.
Truth flows down: if none are, then (assuming there are birdwatchers) some are not.

blocks.title: Truth does not flow up
blocks.q: "Some musicians are painters" is true. What follows about "All musicians are painters"?
steps: I is the subaltern of A.
Truth flows down, not up. Some being painters fits both "all are" and "only some are".

blocks.html: Sending truth up the square: "Some S are P" being true does not make "All S are P" true. Check with a case where only some S are P: the I is true and the A false, so the I alone could not decide the A.
Subalternation depends on the subject class having members. On the modern reading it fails, as a later lesson shows.

blocks.html: Now put the four relations of the square to work. Given that one corner is true or false, you can work out each of the other three as true, false or undetermined.

Start with the contradictory: it always gets the opposite value. Then use the contraries (not both true), subcontraries (not both false) and subalterns (truth down, falsity up) from both the given corner and its contradictory. Whatever is still unsettled is undetermined.

Four of the eight starting cases settle every corner: A true, E true, I false and O false. Each is a strong claim (all, none, not even one, not even one is not), and it pins down the whole square. The other four, A false, E false, I true and O true, are weak claims: they fit the mixed case where some S are P and some are not, and also one extreme case, so two corners stay undetermined.

blocks.title: A weak starting point
blocks.q: "All climbers are hikers" is false. Find E, I and O.
steps: O is the contradictory of A, so O is true.
E: A is false, and contraries can both be false, so A says nothing about E; O (true) is the subaltern of E, and truth does not flow up. E is undetermined.
I: falsity does not flow down from A; O is true, and subcontraries can both be true. I is undetermined.

blocks.title: A strong starting point
blocks.q: "Some dancers are golfers" is false. Find A, E and O.
steps: E is the contradictory of I: true.
Falsity flows up from I to A: A is false.
I and O cannot both be false, so O is true (also, truth flows down from E).
blocks.a: A false, E true, O true

blocks.html: Forcing a value when the honest answer is "undetermined", especially for corners linked only by subalternation or subcontrariety. Check by building a world: if one situation makes the corner true and another makes it false, while the given value holds in both, it is undetermined.

blocks.html: Everything on the square so far used the traditional assumption that the subject class has members. On the modern reading, universal statements have no existential import, and most of the square comes apart.
On the modern (Boolean) square, only the contradictories hold: A–O and E–I still have opposite values. Contrariety, subcontrariety and subalternation can all fail when the subject class is empty.

Suppose there are no dragons. "All dragons breathe fire" and "No dragons breathe fire" say only that two regions are empty, and with no dragons both are true: contrariety fails. "Some dragons breathe fire" and "Some dragons do not" both say a dragon exists, so both are false: subcontrariety fails. And the true A does not send truth down to the false I: subalternation fails. The diagonals survive because each pair still talks about the same region, empty or not.

blocks.name: lg-square
blocks.cap: The modern square: from A true only O (false) follows.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: If the dragons circle is empty, both diagrams are correct at once.

blocks.title: Subalternation on the modern square
blocks.q: On the Boolean reading, "All campers are dancers" is true. What is "Some campers are dancers"?
steps: A and I are not contradictories, so the modern square links them by nothing.
If there are no campers, I is false; if there are, I is true.

blocks.title: A contradictory still works
blocks.q: On the Boolean reading, "Some actors are poets" is false. What is "No actors are poets"?
steps: E and I are contradictories, which hold on every reading.
I is false, so E is true.

blocks.html: Why keep both squares? The traditional square is right whenever we already know the subject class has members, which is true of most everyday talk. The modern square is safer in general, because it makes no assumption, and it is the one built into modern symbolic logic.

Keeping subalternation on the Boolean reading: from "All dragons breathe fire" it does not follow that some dragon breathes fire. Check: could the subject class be empty? If so, the universal is true and the particular false.

blocks.html: An immediate inference draws a conclusion from a single proposition, with no second premise. Before we can make the three classic ones, we need one more idea about classes. In a Venn diagram, everything outside a circle forms a class too.
The complement of a class is everything that is not in it, written with "non-": the complement of winners is non-winners. The complement of non-winners is winners again.

A class and its complement split the whole world in two with nothing left over and nothing counted twice: each thing is either a winner or not. Opposite words do not do that. "Losers" leaves out everyone who never played, and some people are neither. Because a complement leaves no gap, swapping a statement about P for one about non-P can keep the meaning exactly, which is what obversion and contraposition will do.

blocks.name: lg-sort

cards.why: She ran but did not win.
Not a winner, and not a loser either: he never ran.

cards.text: the relay team that won the final

cards.why: Everything that is not a winner is a non-winner.

blocks.cap: Every single thing lands in exactly one of the two groups.

blocks.title: Complement or opposite?
blocks.q: Is "children" the complement of "adults"?
steps: The complement of adults is everything that is not an adult: non-adults.
Teenagers are neither adults nor (in everyday speech) children, and a table is neither. So "children" leaves things out.

blocks.title: Two complements
blocks.q: What is the complement of "non-members"?
steps: The complement is everything outside the class of non-members.
Everything that is not a non-member is a member.

blocks.html: In a two-circle Venn diagram, the class non-P is everything outside the P circle: region 1 (S only) and region 4 (outside both). That is why statements about non-P can be drawn on the same picture as statements about P.

Using the opposite word instead of the complement: the complement of "winners" is "non-winners", not "losers", since some may not have played. Check: is there anything that is neither? If so, the opposite word is not the complement.

blocks.html: Conversion is the simplest immediate inference: swap the subject and predicate terms. Whether it is valid depends on the form, and distribution explains which.

head: Original
Converse
Valid?
blocks.cap: Conversion is valid for E and I only.

blocks.html: Conversion is valid for E and I, which treat both terms alike. It is not valid for A or O. On the traditional reading, A converts by limitation: from "All S are P" to "Some P are S".

In a Venn diagram, E shades the overlap and I puts an X in the overlap. The overlap belongs to both circles equally, so swapping the circles leaves the same picture: same picture, same meaning. A shades the part of S outside P, but its converse shades the part of P outside S, a different region. Distribution says the same: A distributes S but not P, so after the swap P would be distributed without the original statement giving us anything about all P.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: E converts: the two diagrams match.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: A does not: different regions are shaded.

blocks.title: A valid conversion
blocks.q: Convert "Some bakers are anglers". Is the converse equivalent?
steps: Swap the terms: "Some anglers are bakers".
It is an I statement, and I converts validly: both say something is both a baker and an angler.

blocks.title: Conversion by limitation
blocks.q: On the traditional reading, what follows from "All early risers are drummers" by conversion by limitation?
steps: Plain conversion ("All drummers are early risers") does not follow.
Swap the terms and weaken "all" to "some": I.
It needs the traditional assumption that there are early risers.

blocks.html: Converting an A proposition: "All cats are animals" does not give "All animals are cats". This illicit conversion is one of the most common mistakes in reasoning. Check: does the converse claim something about every member of a class the original only partly covered? Then it says more than the original.

blocks.html: Obversion uses complements to say the same thing in the opposite quality. It works for every form.
To obvert: (1) change the quality (affirmative ↔ negative: A ↔ E, I ↔ O) and (2) replace the predicate with its complement. The obverse always means the same as the original.

head: Original
Obverse
blocks.cap: Change the quality, complement the predicate.

blocks.html: The two changes cancel each other, like two negations. "All S are P" says no S lies outside P. "Outside P" is exactly "in non-P", so it says no S are non-P. Saying an S is not in non-P is the same as saying it is in P, because P and non-P split everything with no gap and no overlap.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: A statement and its obverse have the same diagram.

blocks.title: Obverting an E
blocks.q: Obvert "No coders are musicians".
steps: Change the quality: E becomes A ("All … are").
Complement the predicate: musicians → non-musicians.

blocks.title: Removing a "non-"
blocks.q: Obvert "No cyclists are non-debaters".
steps: Change the quality: E becomes A.
Complement the predicate: the complement of non-debaters is debaters.

blocks.html: Obversion is the main tool for removing a "non-" from an argument. When a syllogism seems to have four terms because one of them is a complement, obverting a premise often brings it back to three (you will use this in Unit 6).

Doing only half the job: changing the quality but forgetting to complement the predicate ("No S are P" from "All S are P" means something very different), or complementing the subject instead of the predicate. Check: the subject term must come through untouched, and exactly one "not" or "no" is added or removed.

blocks.html: Contraposition combines the swap of conversion with the complements of obversion.
To contrapose: swap the subject and predicate and replace both with their complements. "All S are P" becomes "All non-P are non-S". Contraposition is valid for A and O, not for E or I.

head: Original
Contrapositive
Valid?
blocks.cap: Contraposition works exactly where conversion fails.

blocks.html: Contraposition is three steps in one: obvert, convert, obvert. Start with "All S are P". Obvert: "No S are non-P". Convert (E converts validly): "No non-P are S". Obvert again: "All non-P are non-S". Every step kept the meaning. Try the same with "No S are P": obverting gives an A, and A does not convert, so the chain breaks. That is why A and O contrapose, and E and I do not.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: A and its contrapositive: the same diagram.

blocks.title: Contraposing an A
blocks.q: Contrapose "All coders are skaters".
steps: Swap: skaters, coders.
Complement both: non-skaters, non-coders.
A contraposes validly.

blocks.title: An invalid contraposition
blocks.q: Does "No non-jugglers are non-knitters" follow from "No knitters are jugglers"?
steps: It is the contrapositive of an E statement.
E does not contrapose: the original shades the knitter–juggler overlap, while the contrapositive shades the region outside both circles.

blocks.html: On the traditional reading, an E statement can be contraposed by limitation: from "No S are P" to "Some non-P are not non-S", just as an A statement converts by limitation. Like every limitation, it needs the assumption that the classes involved have members.
Using contraposition on E or I, or swapping the terms without complementing them (which is only conversion). Check: both terms changed places, both gained or lost "non-", and the form is A or O.

blocks.html: The steps of contraposition, obversion and conversion can be chained, and combined with the square of opposition. A chain lets you decide whether one statement follows from another even when the two look nothing alike.

A chain is valid only if every step is valid for the form it is applied to: obversion for any form, conversion for E and I, contraposition for A and O (and, on the traditional reading only, subalternation and conversion by limitation).

head: Step
Works on
rows: any form, any reading: it gives the opposite truth value
blocks.cap: Check the form before every step.

blocks.html: Each valid step produces a statement with the same meaning (or, for the traditional steps, one that is guaranteed true when the original is). Linking statements that each mean the same as the one before gives a last statement that means the same as the first. One invalid step anywhere breaks the guarantee, even if the remaining steps are fine.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: The start and the end of a chain: same diagram, same meaning.

blocks.title: A two-step chain
blocks.q: If "No poets are campers" is true, must "All campers are non-poets" be true?
steps: Obvert the original (any form): "All poets are non-campers".
That is an A, so contraposition is allowed: "All non-non-campers are non-poets", that is, "All campers are non-poets".

blocks.title: A broken chain
blocks.q: Does "Some non-P are S" follow from "All S are P"?
steps: Obvert: "No S are non-P". Convert (E is fine): "No non-P are S".
That says no non-P are S, the opposite of what was asked.
No valid chain reaches "Some non-P are S"; in fact it is the contradictory of a statement that does follow.

blocks.html: Losing track of the form and slipping in an invalid step, such as converting an A halfway through a chain. Check: write the letter of each line before choosing the next step.

blocks.html: We now reach the third act of the mind, reasoning. In Premises and Conclusions you found premises and conclusions. A categorical syllogism is an argument with exactly two premises and a conclusion, all three of them categorical propositions, using exactly three terms, each used twice.
The conclusion decides the names. Its predicate is the major term (P); its subject is the minor term (S). The term in both premises but not in the conclusion is the middle term (M).

The middle term is the go-between. The conclusion claims some relation between S and P, and the premises can only support it by relating each of them to a third class. If S is tied to M and M is tied to P in the right way, the tie carries over to S and P, and then M disappears from the conclusion. That is why each term appears exactly twice: S and P once in a premise and once in the conclusion, M once in each premise.

blocks.name: lg-syllogism
blocks.cap: S (minor term) in orange, P (major term) in blue, M (middle term) in green.

blocks.title: Naming the terms
blocks.q: Name the major, minor and middle terms: "Some readers are runners. All runners are early risers. So some readers are early risers."
steps: Start with the conclusion: "Some readers are early risers".
Its predicate, early risers, is the major term (P). Its subject, readers, is the minor term (S).
Runners appears in both premises and not in the conclusion: the middle term (M).
blocks.a: major: early risers; minor: readers; middle: runners

blocks.html: Naming the major term by size ("animals" sounds bigger) or by which premise comes first. Only the conclusion decides: its predicate is the major term, its subject the minor term, whatever order the premises were spoken in.
The names come from Aristotle: in his first figure the major term is usually the widest class and the minor term the narrowest. The rule we use (look at the conclusion) works for every syllogism.

blocks.html: Once you can name the three terms, you can put any syllogism in a fixed order. That order is what the names mood and figure describe, so it comes first.
Standard form: the major premise (the premise with the major term) first, then the minor premise (the premise with the minor term), then the conclusion.

A fixed order turns every syllogism into the same pattern, so two arguments with the same pattern can be recognized at once, even when their words differ. People speak arguments in any order ("We will be late, since the bus is slow and…"). Putting the conclusion last and the major premise first is like writing a fraction in lowest terms: a standard way to write the same thing, so that comparing is easy.

items: Find the conclusion (look for so, therefore, since, because).
Its predicate is the major term: the premise containing it is the major premise.
The other premise, which contains the minor term, is the minor premise.
Write: major premise, minor premise, conclusion.

blocks.name: lg-syllogism
blocks.cap: Given in either order, the premises are shown in standard form: the major premise (with "cyclists") on top.

blocks.title: Conclusion first
blocks.q: Put in standard form: "Some volunteers are not cyclists, because no cyclists are coders and some coders are volunteers."
steps: "Because" marks the premises, so the conclusion is "Some volunteers are not cyclists".
Major term: cyclists. The major premise is "No cyclists are coders".
Minor premise: "Some coders are volunteers".
blocks.a: No cyclists are coders / Some coders are volunteers / ∴ Some volunteers are not cyclists

blocks.title: Premises in the wrong order
blocks.q: Which is the major premise? "All squares are rectangles. All rectangles are polygons. Therefore all squares are polygons."
steps: Conclusion: "All squares are polygons". Its predicate, polygons, is the major term.
The premise containing "polygons" is "All rectangles are polygons", although it was spoken second.

blocks.html: Keeping the order in which the premises were spoken. Find the conclusion first, then put the premise with its predicate on top. Check: the first line of your standard form must contain the last word-group of the conclusion.

blocks.html: Every proposition in a standard-form syllogism is an A, E, I or O. Reading the three letters gives a short name for the argument's shape.
The mood of a syllogism is the letters of its major premise, minor premise and conclusion, in that order: for example AAA, EIO or OAO.

Validity depends only on the pattern, never on what the terms are about. Two syllogisms with the same letters in the same positions have the same pattern of all/some and is/is not, so the mood (together with the figure, next lesson) is enough to decide whether an argument is valid. With 4 choices for each of 3 lines there are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 moods.

blocks.name: lg-syllogism
blocks.cap: E, I, O: the mood is EIO.

blocks.title: Reorder, then read
blocks.q: Find the mood: "Some potters are knitters. All knitters are gardeners. So some potters are gardeners."
steps: The conclusion's predicate is gardeners, so the major premise is "All knitters are gardeners": A.
The minor premise is "Some potters are knitters": I.
The conclusion "Some potters are gardeners" is I.

blocks.title: Conclusion first
blocks.q: Find the mood: "Some swimmers are not drummers, since no drummers are artists and some swimmers are artists."
steps: The conclusion comes first here: "Some swimmers are not drummers" (O). Its predicate, drummers, is the major term.
Major premise: "No drummers are artists" (E). Minor premise: "Some swimmers are artists" (I).
Standard order: E, I, O.

blocks.html: A mood alone does not settle validity. EIO happens to be valid in every figure, but AAA is valid only in figure 1: "All P are M, all S are M, so all S are P" is not. The next lesson adds the figure.

Reading the letters in the order the sentences appear rather than in standard-form order. In the example above, the spoken order gives IAI, a different mood. Check: the first letter must belong to the premise with the major term.

blocks.html: The mood does not tell the whole shape of a syllogism. "All M are P" and "All P are M" are both A, but they place the middle term differently. The figure records where the middle term sits.

head: Figure
Major premise
Minor premise
Middle term is…
blocks.cap: The four figures (premises in standard order).

blocks.html: Figure 1: the middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor. Figure 2: predicate of both. Figure 3: subject of both. Figure 4: predicate of the major, subject of the minor. The form of a syllogism is its mood and figure, such as AII-3.

The figure matters because it changes which terms are distributed where. "All M are P" distributes M, but "All P are M" does not. With 64 moods and 4 figures there are 256 forms, and each one is either always valid or never valid, whatever its terms.

blocks.cap: Middle term "birds": subject of the major premise, predicate of the minor: figure 1. Form AAA-1.

blocks.title: Figure 2
blocks.q: Find the figure: "No mammals are reptiles. All snakes are reptiles. So no snakes are mammals."
steps: The conclusion's predicate is mammals, so "No mammals are reptiles" is the major premise. The middle term is reptiles.
In the major premise, M is the predicate.
In the minor premise "All snakes are reptiles", M is the predicate again.
Predicate twice is figure 2.

blocks.title: Figure 3
blocks.q: Find the figure: "All knitters are climbers. All knitters are runners. So some runners are climbers."
steps: Middle term: knitters.
It is the subject of both premises.

blocks.html: Mixing up figures 1 and 4. In figure 1 the middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor (M–P, S–M); figure 4 is the reverse (P–M, M–S). Check: put the premises in standard order first, then trace where M sits in each line.

blocks.html: A syllogism is about three classes, so its picture needs three circles: S on the left, P on the right, M below. They make eight regions. You already know how to diagram one proposition; now you diagram two.
Diagram only the premises. The syllogism is valid if the picture then already shows the conclusion, with nothing more drawn. If you would have to add something, it is invalid.

A valid argument is one where the premises cannot be true while the conclusion is false. The diagram of the premises shows everything the premises say, and nothing more. If the conclusion is already in that picture, every situation that fits the premises fits the conclusion too, which is exactly validity. If the conclusion needs one more mark, then a situation fitting the premises but not the conclusion is possible.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: Celarent, EAE-1: step through the premises. The golfer–camper overlap ends up fully shaded, so the conclusion is shown.

blocks.title: A valid syllogism
blocks.q: Test: "No bakers are campers. All golfers are bakers. So no golfers are campers." (S = golfers, P = campers, M = bakers)
steps: Premise 1: no bakers are campers. Shade the overlap of M and P (regions 5 and 6).
Premise 2: all golfers are bakers. Shade the part of S outside M (regions 1 and 2).
The conclusion says the overlap of S and P (regions 2 and 5) is empty. Both are already shaded.

blocks.title: An invalid one with true statements
blocks.q: Test: "All squares are polygons. All squares are rectangles. So all rectangles are polygons." (S = rectangles, P = polygons, M = squares)
steps: Premise 1 shades the part of M outside P (regions 4 and 7). Premise 2 shades the part of M outside S (regions 6 and 7).
The conclusion needs the part of S outside P (regions 1 and 4) empty. Region 4 is shaded, but region 1 is not.
Every statement is true, yet the picture does not show the conclusion.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: Region 1 stays open: the conclusion is not shown, so the form is invalid even though every statement is true.

blocks.html: Diagramming the conclusion too, then saying the picture "matches". Only the premises are drawn; then you read the conclusion off the picture. Check: before reading, count your marks. There should be exactly one mark (or one pair of shaded regions) per premise.

sources.name: Patrick J. Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, 5.2 Venn Diagrams

blocks.html: With an I or O premise, the Venn test needs an X, and the X needs care: a premise like "Some S are M" says something is in the S–M overlap, but that overlap is cut in two by the P circle.

Diagram universal premises first. Then place the X for a particular premise: in a region if only one of its two regions is still open, or on the line between them if both are open. An X on a line does not show that something is on either side.

Shading first can settle where the X must go: if one half of the overlap is already empty, the something must be in the other half. Doing the X first would force a guess. And when both halves are open, the premise leaves it unknown which half holds the thing, so the X sits on the line. Putting it on one side would add information the premises never gave.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: Darii, AII-1: shade first, and the X has only one place to go (region 5).

blocks.title: Shade first
blocks.q: Test: "All athletes are readers. Some students are athletes. So some students are readers." (S = students, P = readers, M = athletes)
steps: Universal premise first: no athletes outside the readers. Shade regions 4 and 7.
Particular premise: something is a student and an athlete, regions 4 or 5. Region 4 is shaded, so the X goes in region 5.
The conclusion needs an X in the student–reader overlap (regions 2 or 5). There is one in region 5.

blocks.title: An X on the line
blocks.q: Test: "All painters are bakers. Some golfers are bakers. So some golfers are painters." (S = golfers, P = painters, M = bakers)
steps: Shade the part of the painters circle outside the bakers: regions 2 and 3.
Some golfers are bakers: regions 4 or 5, both open, so the X goes on the line between them.
The conclusion needs an X in region 2 or 5. The X might be in region 4 instead.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: The X sits on the line between regions 4 and 5, so the conclusion is not shown.

blocks.html: Dropping the X into one region when the premise allows two. That adds information and can make an invalid syllogism look valid. Check: for each X, ask "Did a premise force this side?" If not, it belongs on the line.

blocks.html: Venn diagrams test one syllogism at a time. Rules test by looking at distribution and quality, and they also name what went wrong. The first two rules are about distribution.

items: Rule 1: the middle term must be distributed at least once. Breaking it: undistributed middle.
Rule 2: a term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise. Breaking it: illicit major (for P) or illicit minor (for S).

blocks.html: Mark the distributed terms (A: subject; E: both; I: neither; O: predicate). The middle term needs a mark in at least one premise, and every term marked in the conclusion needs a mark in its premise.

Rule 1: if neither premise speaks of all of M, the premises may be about different parts of M, and then nothing links S to P. Rule 2: a conclusion that speaks of every P (or every S) claims more than a premise that spoke only of some of them. A conclusion can never say more about a class than the premises said.

blocks.name: lg-syllogism
blocks.cap: "Mammals" is the predicate of two A statements, so it is never distributed: undistributed middle.

blocks.title: Undistributed middle
blocks.q: Which rule does this break? "All dogs are mammals. All cats are mammals. So all cats are dogs."
steps: Distributed terms: premise 1, dogs; premise 2, cats; conclusion, cats.
The middle term mammals is distributed in neither premise.
The dogs and the cats may be different parts of the mammals.

blocks.title: Illicit major
blocks.q: Which rule does this break? "All early risers are climbers. No singers are early risers. So no singers are climbers."
steps: The conclusion is E, so both singers and climbers are distributed in it.
The major term climbers appears in the major premise as the predicate of an A statement: not distributed.

blocks.html: Undistributed middle: "All dogs are animals; all cats are animals; so all cats are dogs." Both premises talk about only part of the animals. Check: underline the middle term each time it is distributed. If it has no underline, stop: the syllogism is invalid.

sources.name: Patrick J. Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, 5.3 Rules and Fallacies

blocks.html: The distribution rules are two of six. The next three are about quality, that is, about the negative statements (E and O).

items: Rule 3: two negative premises are not allowed. Breaking it: exclusive premises.

Rule 4: a negative premise requires a negative conclusion, and a negative conclusion requires a negative premise. Breaking it: affirmative conclusion from a negative premise, or negative conclusion from affirmative premises.

blocks.html: Count the negatives. Zero negative premises: the conclusion must be affirmative. Exactly one: the conclusion must be negative. Two: the syllogism is invalid.

A negative premise says that M excludes something. If both premises only say what M excludes, they never say what M includes, so S and P are never brought together and nothing follows about them. With one negative premise, one of S or P is linked to M and the other is shut out of M, so the only link that can follow is an exclusion: a negative conclusion. And affirmative premises only include classes in one another; they cannot produce an exclusion.

blocks.name: lg-syllogism
blocks.cap: Two negative premises: exclusive premises. (The premises are true and the conclusion false.)

blocks.title: Exclusive premises
blocks.q: Is this valid? "No fish are mammals. No whales are fish. So no whales are mammals."
steps: Both premises are negative (E, E).
They say only what the fish exclude, so they never connect whales and mammals.
Here the premises are true and the conclusion false, which no valid form allows.

blocks.title: Affirmative from a negative
blocks.q: Which quality rule does this break? "No poets are hikers. All hikers are skaters. So some skaters are poets."
steps: One negative premise (E).
The conclusion (I) is affirmative.
blocks.a: affirmative conclusion from a negative premise

blocks.html: Thinking two negative premises can still link the terms ("No cats are dogs; no dogs are birds; so no cats are birds" sounds right). If neither premise says what the middle term includes, the terms never meet. Check: count the E and O premises first; two means stop.

sources.name: Patrick J. Hurley, A Concise Introduction to Logic, 5.3 Rules and Fallacies

blocks.html: Put the distribution rules and the quality rules together with one more, and you have the six rules for a standard-form syllogism (on the modern reading). Each broken rule has a name.

head: Rule
Fallacy when broken
rows: 1. The middle term is distributed at least once.
2. A term distributed in the conclusion is distributed in its premise.
4. A negative premise needs a negative conclusion, and the reverse.
Affirmative conclusion from a negative premise / negative conclusion from affirmative premises
5. (Modern reading) Two universal premises cannot give a particular conclusion.
A syllogism must have exactly three terms.
blocks.cap: The rules and their fallacies.

blocks.html: A syllogism is valid (modern reading) exactly when it breaks none of the rules. Check every rule: one syllogism can break several, and each name points to a different flaw.

The existential fallacy is the rule we have not met yet. On the modern reading, universal premises say only that regions are empty, so they put no X in the diagram. A particular conclusion needs an X. So two universal premises can never prove a particular conclusion, unless we add the traditional assumption that some class has members (the last lesson of this unit).

blocks.name: lg-syllogism
blocks.cap: Two rules broken at once: illicit major and negative conclusion from affirmative premises.

blocks.title: Two fallacies
blocks.q: Name every fallacy: "All bakers are skaters. All early risers are bakers. So no early risers are skaters."
steps: Distribution: the conclusion (E) distributes skaters, but the major premise (A) does not: illicit major.
Quality: both premises affirmative, conclusion negative: negative conclusion from affirmative premises.
The middle term is distributed (premise 1) and the minor term is fine.
blocks.a: illicit major; negative conclusion from affirmative premises

blocks.title: Four terms
blocks.q: What is wrong with: "All chess players are thinkers. All chess fans are viewers. So all chess players are viewers"?
steps: Count the terms: chess players, thinkers, chess fans, viewers. That is four.
With no shared middle term, the premises cannot connect anything.

blocks.html: Stopping at the first broken rule. The question "which fallacies?" wants all of them. Check all five rules in order (middle, major, minor, the negatives, universals to a particular) every time.

Validity belongs to the form, so a short list of forms covers every valid syllogism ever written. Each name was checked once, and every argument with the same mood and figure inherits the result. You can confirm any entry with a Venn diagram or the rules; the names only save you the work.

steps: Major premise "All runners are early risers": A. Minor "Some runners are readers": I. Conclusion: I. Mood AII.
The middle term runners is the subject of both premises: figure 3.

blocks.q: Write Camestres with S, P and M.
steps: The vowels a, e, e give AEE. Camestres is in figure 2 (P–M, S–M).
Major: All P are M. Minor: No S are M. Conclusion: No S are P.

blocks.html: The fifteen valid forms assume nothing about existence. On the traditional reading, where classes are assumed to have members, nine more forms become valid. They are called conditionally valid.

head: Form
Name
Class that must have members
blocks.cap: The nine conditionally valid forms.

blocks.html: A conditionally valid form commits the existential fallacy on the modern reading, but it is valid if one particular class has at least one member. The Venn test shows which class: the one whose circle has its only open part inside the region the conclusion needs.

Each of these forms has two universal premises and a particular conclusion. The premises shade regions but draw no X, and the conclusion needs an X. Now assume a class has members. If the shading leaves that circle open only inside the conclusion's region, the member must be there, which puts the X right where the conclusion needs it. Assuming a different class may not help, so the choice of class matters.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: AAI-1 (Barbari): with the assumption that there are S, the only open part of S is region 5, inside the conclusion's region.

blocks.title: Barbari
blocks.q: "All mammals are animals. All whales are mammals. So some whales are animals." Valid on which reading?
steps: AAI-1: two universals, a particular conclusion. On the modern reading: existential fallacy.
Assume there are whales (S). The shading leaves only the whale–mammal–animal region open in the whale circle, so a whale must be there.
So it is valid on the traditional reading, if there are whales.
blocks.a: conditionally valid: S must have members

blocks.title: Darapti
blocks.q: For AAI-3, "All M are P. All M are S. So some S are P", which class must have members?
steps: Assuming S helps? The S circle still has open parts outside P (region 1), so no.
Assume M has members: both premises shade every part of M except the region inside S and P (region 5). The X goes there.

blocks.html: Counting AAI-1 as valid on the modern reading. It needs the assumption that the minor term's class is not empty, or it commits the existential fallacy. Check: two universal premises with a particular conclusion always need an existence assumption.

blocks.html: A syllogism must have exactly three terms. Real arguments often seem to have more: one premise says "students" and another "pupils", or one says "players" and another "non-players". Before calling it the fallacy of four terms, try to reduce the number of terms with tools you already have: synonyms, complements and obversion, and then put it in standard form.

Replace synonyms with one word. When a term appears with and without "non-", rewrite a premise (by obversion, or by contraposition for A and O) so the "non-" disappears. If three terms remain, test the syllogism as usual.

Rewriting is allowed because the new statement means exactly the same as the old one. Synonyms name the same class; obversion and valid contraposition give equivalent statements. Changing the words without changing the claims cannot change whether the argument is valid, so the reduced syllogism stands or falls with the original.

head: Seems like
Rewrite
Why it is allowed

blocks.name: lg-syllogism
blocks.cap: After reducing the first example below: AOO-2, Baroko, valid.

blocks.title: Removing a complement
blocks.q: Reduce to three terms and test: "No bakers are non-anglers. Some sailors are not anglers. So some sailors are not bakers."
steps: Four apparent terms: bakers, non-anglers, sailors, anglers. But non-anglers is the complement of anglers.
Obvert premise 1: change the quality and complement the predicate. "No bakers are non-anglers" becomes "All bakers are anglers".
Now: All bakers are anglers / Some sailors are not anglers / ∴ Some sailors are not bakers. That is AOO-2 (Baroko).

blocks.title: Synonyms and contraposition
blocks.q: Reduce and test: "All non-runners are non-athletes. All pupils on the team are athletes. So all students on the team are runners."
steps: "Pupils on the team" and "students on the team" are synonyms: use one phrase.
Contrapose premise 1 (an A statement): "All athletes are runners".
Now: All athletes are runners / All students on the team are athletes / ∴ All students on the team are runners. That is AAA-1 (Barbara).

blocks.html: Calling an argument invalid for four terms when two of its terms are synonyms or complements, or the reverse: treating two terms as the same when the meaning has shifted ("light" as in weight and "light" as in color). Check: do the two words name exactly the same class, or exact complements? Only then may you merge them.

blocks.html: Arguments in conversation, ads and articles use everyday words. Testing them takes everything from this course so far: standard form, "only", reducing terms, and then a Venn diagram or the rules.

items: Find the conclusion (indicator words help).
Translate each statement into standard form; watch "only", "not every" and verbs.
Reduce to three terms if needed.
Arrange in standard form and find the mood and figure.
Test with the rules or a Venn diagram.

blocks.html: Translate first, then test. Every judgment about validity is made on the standard-form version.

Everyday wording hides the form. "Only members may vote" looks like it starts with the subject "members", but its standard form puts members in the predicate. If you test the wording instead of the meaning, you test the wrong argument. Translation is where most mistakes happen, so it gets its own step before any testing.

blocks.name: lg-venn3
blocks.cap: Darii after translation: the X lands in region 5, inside the potter–volunteer overlap.

blocks.title: A hidden "only"
blocks.q: Is this valid? "Only people with a ticket can enter the gym. Some parents can enter the gym. So some parents are people with a ticket."
steps: "Only people with a ticket can enter" → All people who can enter the gym are people with a ticket.
"Some parents can enter" → Some parents are people who can enter the gym.
Conclusion: Some parents are people with a ticket. Middle term: people who can enter the gym.
Standard form: All M are P / Some S are M / ∴ Some S are P. That is AII-1, Darii.

blocks.title: Not every
blocks.q: Is this valid? "Not every birdwatcher is a skater. None of the skaters are drummers. Hence there are birdwatchers who are not drummers."
steps: Translate: Some birdwatchers are not skaters (O). No skaters are drummers (E). Some birdwatchers are not drummers (O).
Two negative premises.

blocks.html: Testing before translating, or translating "only" the wrong way round. Reversing "only" turns "All people who enter are ticket holders" into "All ticket holders enter", and that flips a valid argument into an invalid one (or the reverse). Check: write the standard form of every line before you look for the middle term.

blocks.html: In Unstated Premises you saw that people leave obvious premises unsaid. A syllogism with a premise or the conclusion left out is called an enthymeme. To evaluate it, you first supply the missing part, and test it like any syllogism.
Supply the missing statement that makes the syllogism valid and is as plausible as possible. Then judge the whole argument: valid, and are the premises (including the one you supplied) true?

A fair reader fills the gap the way the speaker most likely meant it: with a premise that makes the reasoning work. Supplying a premise that makes the argument invalid would attack a position nobody held. But the supplied premise must also be believable; choosing a claim that is stronger than needed and plainly false would be unfair in the other direction.

blocks.name: lg-argmap
blocks.cap: The unstated premise joins the stated one to make a valid syllogism (EIO-2, Festino).

blocks.title: A missing premise
blocks.q: Supply the missing premise: "Some swimmers are cyclists, so some swimmers are not knitters."
steps: The conclusion's terms are swimmers (S) and knitters (P). The stated premise uses swimmers and cyclists, so cyclists is the middle term.
The missing premise must link cyclists and knitters, and since the conclusion is negative, it must be negative.
"No knitters are cyclists" gives EIO-2 (Festino), which is valid. ("No cyclists are knitters" says the same.)

blocks.title: Weak or strong?
blocks.q: Supply a premise: "Leo is invited on the hike, because all the campers are invited."
steps: In standard form: All campers are invited people / ∴ All people identical to Leo are invited people. The missing premise links Leo and campers.
"All people identical to Leo are campers" (Leo is a camper) makes it Barbara, valid.
A stronger premise such as "Everyone in town is a camper" would also work, but it is plainly false. The fair choice is the weaker, plausible one.

blocks.html: Supplying a premise that makes the syllogism invalid (such as "All cyclists are knitters" in the first example, which leaves two affirmative premises with a negative conclusion), or one so strong that it is plainly false when a weaker true one would work. Check: test the completed syllogism, then ask if the premise you added is believable.

blocks.html: A sorites is a chain of three or more premises leading to one conclusion. It packs several enthymemes together: each step produces an unstated intermediate conclusion that becomes a premise of the next step.
A sorites is valid when every link in the chain is a valid syllogism. To test it, put the premises in chain order, draw each intermediate conclusion, and test each link.

Each link takes the conclusion so far and one new premise, and produces a new conclusion. If every link is valid, the truth of the premises passes along the chain like a relay, all the way to the end. One bad link breaks the relay: what comes after it is no longer guaranteed, even if every later link is fine.

blocks.name: lg-argmap
blocks.cap: Two links, each Barbara. The middle box is the hidden intermediate conclusion.

blocks.title: Ordering the chain
blocks.q: What follows? "All anglers are bakers. All actors are climbers. All climbers are anglers."
steps: Find the term that is never a predicate: actors. Start there: All actors are climbers.
Next, the premise about climbers: All climbers are anglers. Link 1 (Barbara): All actors are anglers.
Then the premise about anglers: All anglers are bakers. Link 2 (Barbara): All actors are bakers.

blocks.title: A negative last link
blocks.q: What follows? "All poets are hikers. No singers are runners. All hikers are singers."
steps: Chain: poets → hikers → singers, then "no singers are runners".
Link 1: All poets are hikers, all hikers are singers, so all poets are singers (Barbara).
Link 2: No singers are runners, all poets are singers, so no poets are runners (Celarent).

blocks.html: Lewis Carroll, the author of Alice in Wonderland, wrote famous sorites puzzles with silly premises, such as chains about babies, crocodiles and logic. Silly premises are a good reminder that validity is about form, not about whether the premises are true.

Checking only the first and last premises. Each step in the chain must be a valid syllogism on its own; one undistributed middle in the middle of the chain breaks the whole sorites. Check: write out every intermediate conclusion and test each link.

blocks.html: Not every proposition is categorical. A hypothetical proposition joins two whole statements with "if": "If it rains, then the game is canceled." The part after "if" is the antecedent; the part after "then" is the consequent. You met these in Affirming the Consequent and Denying the Antecedent.
"If P, then Q" says that P is enough for Q. "Q if P", "Q provided that P", "Whenever P, Q" and "P only if Q" all say the same thing: P is the antecedent and Q the consequent.

"P only if Q" says that P cannot happen without Q: Q is required. So whenever P happens, Q must have happened too, and that is exactly "If P, then Q". "You may drive only if you have a license" means: if you may drive, you have a license. It does not promise that having a license lets you drive (you might also need insurance). The word "only" points to the requirement, which becomes the consequent.

head: Wording
If …, then …
rows: The game is canceled if it rains.
If it rains, then the game is canceled.
You may drive only if you have a license.
If you may drive, then you have a license.
The cake burns whenever it bakes too long.
If the cake bakes too long, then it burns.
A license is necessary for driving.
If you drive, then you have a license.
Rain is sufficient for canceling the game.
If it rains, then the game is canceled.

blocks.q: Rewrite with "If …, then …": "Sam goes to the movies only if Sam finishes his chores."
steps: "Only if" introduces the consequent: Sam finishes his chores.
So the antecedent is "Sam goes to the movies".

blocks.q: Rewrite: "Practice is necessary for making the team."
steps: A necessary condition is a requirement, so it is the consequent.
Antecedent: you make the team.
blocks.a: If you make the team, then you practiced.

blocks.html: Reversing "only if". "P only if Q" means "If P then Q", not "If Q then P". Check with the license example: having a license does not by itself let you drive, so "only if" cannot mean "if you have a license, you may drive".

blocks.html: A hypothetical syllogism has a hypothetical proposition as a premise. The simplest is called modus ponens (Latin: "the way that affirms"), or affirming the antecedent.

head: Form
Example
rows: If the dog hears the doorbell, the dog barks.
blocks.cap: Modus ponens.

blocks.html: From "If P, then Q" and "P", conclude "Q". Modus ponens is valid: whenever both premises are true, the conclusion is true.

"If P, then Q" rules out exactly one situation: P true and Q false. The second premise says P is true. The only situation left is the one where Q is true too. A truth table lists every case at once. Write p for "the dog hears the doorbell" and q for "the dog barks"; the arrow → means "if … then". The only row where both premises are true has q true.

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: Every row where both premises are true (only the first) has the conclusion true: valid.

blocks.title: What follows?
blocks.q: "If Maya finishes her chores, then Maya goes to the movies. Maya finishes her chores." What follows?
steps: The second premise affirms the antecedent.
By modus ponens, the consequent follows.

blocks.title: Order does not matter
blocks.q: Is this modus ponens? "The puddles freeze, since the temperature dropped below freezing, and if the temperature drops below freezing, the puddles freeze."
steps: The conclusion comes first ("since" marks the premises), but the form is the same.
Premises: If P then Q; P. Conclusion: Q.

blocks.html: Rejecting a modus ponens because you doubt the first premise. "If the moon is made of cheese, then mice can live on the moon; the moon is made of cheese; so mice can live on the moon" is valid. Its premises are false, so it is unsound, but the form is fine. Doubting a premise is a question about soundness, not validity.

blocks.html: The second valid hypothetical form runs modus ponens in reverse. Modus tollens ("the way that denies") is also called denying the consequent.

head: Form
Example
rows: If the field is flooded, the game is postponed.
So the field is not flooded.
blocks.cap: Modus tollens.

blocks.html: From "If P, then Q" and "not Q", conclude "not P". Modus tollens is valid.

If P had been true, Q would have been true too; that is what the first premise says. But Q is false. So P cannot have been true. On the truth table (¬ means "not"), the only row where both "p → q" and "¬q" are true is the row with p false. Detectives and scientists use this form all the time: "If the suspect were in the room, there would be footprints. There are none. So the suspect was not in the room."

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: Only the last row makes both premises true, and there ¬p is true: valid.

blocks.title: Denying the consequent
blocks.q: "If the store is open, then the lights are on. The lights are not on." What follows?
steps: The second premise denies the consequent.
By modus tollens, deny the antecedent.

blocks.title: Spotting the form
blocks.q: Is this valid? "If Priya wins the spelling bee, she goes to the state final. She does not go to the state final. So she did not win."
steps: Form: If P then Q; not Q; so not P.
That is modus tollens.

blocks.html: Finding modus tollens harder than modus ponens and wrongly rejecting it. If P would bring Q, and there is no Q, there was no P. Check with a truth table or a plain case: "If it is a square, it has four sides. It does not have four sides. So it is not a square." Clearly right.

head: Form
Pattern
Valid?

If P then Q; not Q; so not P
If P then Q; Q; so P
If P then Q; not P; so not Q
blocks.cap: Two valid forms and their invalid twins.

blocks.html: Affirming the consequent (Q, so P) and denying the antecedent (not P, so not Q) are invalid: the consequent can come about some other way.

"If P, then Q" says P is one way to get Q. It does not say it is the only way. So learning that Q happened does not tell you P happened (affirming the consequent), and learning that P did not happen does not tell you Q failed (denying the antecedent). The truth table shows a counterexample row for each: P false and Q true makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

blocks.cap: Affirming the consequent: the third row (p false, q true) has true premises and a false conclusion.

blocks.title: Affirming the consequent
blocks.q: "If the dog hears the doorbell, it barks. The dog is barking. So it heard the doorbell." Valid?
steps: The second premise affirms the consequent; the conclusion affirms the antecedent.
Counterexample: a squirrel ran past the window. The dog barks, though no doorbell rang.

blocks.title: Denying the antecedent
blocks.q: "If the number is divisible by 4, it is even. This number is not divisible by 4. So it is not even." Valid?
steps: The second premise denies the antecedent.
Counterexample: 6 is not divisible by 4, but it is even.

blocks.html: Affirming the consequent is the most common formal fallacy ("If it rained, the street is wet; the street is wet; so it rained"). Show it with a counterexample where Q is true for a different reason: a street cleaner went by.

blocks.html: In modus ponens only one premise is hypothetical. In a pure hypothetical syllogism, every statement is: the premises link conditionals into a chain.

head: Form
Example
rows: If the alarm rings, Sam wakes up.
If Sam wakes up, Sam catches the bus.
So if the alarm rings, Sam catches the bus.
blocks.cap: Pure hypothetical syllogism (also called hypothetical syllogism, HS).

blocks.html: From "If P, then Q" and "If Q, then R", conclude "If P, then R". The consequent of the first must be the antecedent of the second; the links must run in the same direction.

Imagine P happens. By the first premise, Q happens. By the second, R happens. So whenever P happens, R does: that is "If P, then R". The chain works like the categorical chain in a sorites: Q is the middle term, and it must sit at the end of one link and the start of the next.

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: Three letters, eight rows: no row makes both premises true and the conclusion false.

blocks.title: A longer chain
blocks.q: What follows? "If it snows tonight, school opens late. If the math quiz moves to Friday, Kim has an extra day to study. If school opens late, the math quiz moves to Friday."
steps: Order the links: snow → school opens late → quiz moves to Friday → extra day.
Each consequent is the next antecedent.
blocks.a: If it snows tonight, Kim has an extra day to study.

blocks.title: Links that do not chain
blocks.q: What follows? "If the power goes out, the freezer stops. If the door is left open, the freezer stops."
steps: Both conditionals end at the same consequent.
Nothing runs from "power out" to "door open" or back.
blocks.a: nothing follows about how the two antecedents are related

blocks.html: Chaining conditionals that do not share a middle in the right place, such as "If P then Q" and "If R then Q". Both arrows point into Q, so nothing connects P and R. Check: draw the arrows; you must be able to follow them from start to end without going backward.

blocks.html: Another kind of compound statement uses "or": "Either the keys are in the car or they are on the hook." Each part is a disjunct. Like hypothetical propositions, disjunctions support their own syllogism.
Disjunctive syllogism: from "P or Q" and "not P", conclude "Q" (or from "not Q", conclude "P"). But from "P or Q" and "P", nothing follows about Q, because logic's "or" is inclusive: it allows both.

"P or Q" says at least one is true. Rule one out, and the other must be the true one. But learning that one is true does not rule the other out, since both may be true. "Either Ana is at practice or she is at the library" is not proven false if she went to both. Concluding "not Q" from "P" is the fallacy of affirming a disjunct. It is only safe when the speaker has made clear that the options exclude each other ("either … or …, but not both").

blocks.cap: Disjunctive syllogism: the only row with both premises true has q true. (∨ means "or".)

blocks.name: lg-truthtable
blocks.cap: Affirming a disjunct: the first row (both true) is a counterexample.

blocks.title: Ruling one out
blocks.q: "Either the noise came from the attic or it came from the garage. It did not come from the attic." What follows?
steps: One disjunct is denied.
The other must be true.
blocks.a: The noise came from the garage.

blocks.title: Affirming a disjunct
blocks.q: "Either we take the train or we take the bus. We take the train. So we do not take the bus." Valid?
steps: The second premise affirms one disjunct.
With inclusive "or", we could take both (the train, then a bus).

blocks.html: Reading every "or" as "one or the other but not both". Logic's "or" is inclusive unless the speaker rules out both. Check: could both disjuncts be true at once? If yes, affirming one tells you nothing about the other.

blocks.html: A conjunction joins statements with "and". Its denial, "not both P and Q", says the two cannot be true together. It powers a syllogism much like the disjunctive syllogism, but in the opposite direction.
Conjunctive syllogism: from "Not both P and Q" and "P", conclude "not Q". But from "Not both P and Q" and "not P", nothing follows: "not both" allows neither.

"Not both" rules out exactly one case: both true. If P is true, Q would make that case happen, so Q must be false. But if P is false, the forbidden case is already avoided, and Q is free to be true or false. "Ben is not both at the game and at home" fits Ben being at the library, where he is at neither.

blocks.title: Affirming one part
blocks.q: "It is not the case that both the traffic light is red and the traffic light is green. The light is red." What follows?
steps: "Not both" plus one part true.
The other part must be false.

blocks.title: Denying one part
blocks.q: "Kim is not both the team captain and the team treasurer. Kim is not the captain." What follows about the treasurer?
steps: Denying one part avoids the forbidden case already.
Kim might be the treasurer, or might hold neither job.

blocks.html: Denying one conjunct and concluding the other is true. "Not both" allows neither to be true. Check: is there a situation where both parts are false? If so, the conclusion can fail.
The Stoic logicians of ancient Greece listed this form, together with modus ponens, modus tollens and two disjunctive forms, among their five basic arguments.

blocks.html: A dilemma combines two conditionals with a disjunction. It is the argument of "either way, you lose" (or "either way, you win").

head: Constructive dilemma
Destructive dilemma
rows: If P then Q, and if R then S.
If P then Q, and if R then S.
So not P or not R.
blocks.cap: The two valid dilemmas.

blocks.html: A constructive dilemma affirms the antecedents (P or R) and concludes the consequents (Q or S): modus ponens on each horn. A destructive dilemma denies the consequents and concludes the denial of the antecedents: modus tollens on each horn. Both are valid.

Take the constructive dilemma. At least one of P and R is true. If it is P, the first conditional gives Q; if it is R, the second gives S. Either way, Q or S. The destructive dilemma is the same reasoning with modus tollens. The two options in the "or" premise are called the horns of the dilemma.

blocks.name: lg-argmap

nodes.text: If we leave early, we wait at the gate for an hour.
If we leave late, we miss the opening song.
We leave early or we leave late.
We wait an hour, or we miss the opening song.

blocks.cap: A constructive dilemma: three linked premises.

blocks.title: Constructive
blocks.q: "If Jo studies tonight, Jo misses the concert; if Jo goes to the concert, Jo does poorly on the quiz. Jo studies tonight or goes to the concert." What follows?
steps: The "or" premise affirms the two antecedents.
Constructive dilemma: one consequent or the other.
blocks.a: Jo misses the concert or does poorly on the quiz.

blocks.title: A broken dilemma
blocks.q: "If the family drives, the trip takes two days; if they fly, the trip costs more. The trip takes two days or costs more. So the family drives or flies." Valid?
steps: The "or" premise affirms the consequents, and the conclusion affirms the antecedents.
That is affirming the consequent on each horn: the trip could take two days because of a storm while they take the train.

blocks.html: Mixing the two patterns: affirming consequents in a destructive dilemma or denying antecedents in a constructive one, which makes it invalid. Check: a constructive dilemma moves forward along the arrows (antecedents to consequents); a destructive one moves backward with "not" (denied consequents to denied antecedents).

blocks.html: A dilemma can feel like a trap, but a valid argument is only as good as its premises. Since the classic dilemmas are valid, answering one means challenging a premise. Rhetoric teachers named three ways to do it. (Calling the choice too narrow is the same move you studied in False Dilemma.)

items: Escaping between the horns: show a third option the "or" premise left out, so the disjunction is false.
Grasping a horn: deny one of the conditionals; show that one option does not lead where the arguer claims.
Offering a counterdilemma: build a new dilemma from the same options with a different (often cheerful) conclusion.

blocks.html: A valid dilemma can only be answered by showing that a premise is false or doubtful: the disjunction (between the horns) or a conditional (grasping a horn). A counterdilemma does not refute; it shows another way to look at the same choice.

Validity guarantees that true premises give a true conclusion. So if you want to reject the conclusion, you must find a premise to reject; complaining about the form gets nowhere. Escaping between the horns attacks the "or"; grasping a horn attacks an "if". A counterdilemma leaves both standing and changes the emphasis, which is why it persuades but does not prove the original wrong.

nodes.text: If the club raises its dues, some members quit.
If the club keeps its dues the same, it cannot buy new equipment.
The club raises its dues or keeps them the same.
Some members quit, or the club cannot buy new equipment.
The club could keep its dues the same and hold a bake sale for the equipment.

blocks.cap: The objection attacks the second conditional: grasping a horn.

blocks.title: Between the horns
blocks.q: Dilemma: "If we leave early, we wait an hour; if we leave late, we miss the song; we leave early or late." Reply: "We could leave at a middle time." Which way of answering is it?
steps: The reply offers a third option the "or" premise ignored.
It denies the disjunction.

blocks.title: A counterdilemma
blocks.q: Reply to the same dilemma: "If we leave early, we get the best seats; if we leave late, we skip the long line. Either way, we gain something."
steps: The reply keeps the same two options.
It draws a new, cheerful conclusion from new conditionals.

blocks.html: Answering a valid dilemma by calling it invalid. A valid dilemma can only be answered by showing one of its premises is false. Check: first ask whether the form is a correct constructive or destructive dilemma; if it is, look for a third option or a weak "if … then".
Some dilemmas cannot be escaped between the horns because the options are a statement and its denial ("Either Sam admits it or he keeps quiet"). Then only grasping a horn or a counterdilemma remains.
